q-37357.problem:
Find the characteristic equation of the matrix 
$B=[\begin{aligned}-40 & 6 & 30 \\ 0 & -10 & 0 \\ -80 & 14 & 60\end{aligned}].$
q-37357.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,B-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
B-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-40-\lambda  & 6 & 30 \\ 0 & -10-\lambda  & 0 \\ -80 & 14 & 60-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(B-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $2$nd row, we obtain the following:  

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-40-\lambda  & 6 & 30 \\ 0 & -10-\lambda  & 0 \\ -80 & 14 & 60-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-10-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-40-\lambda  & 30 \\ -80 & 60-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-10-\lambda )((-40-\lambda )(60-\lambda )-(30)(-80)) & =0 \\ (-10-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda ) & =0 \\ (\lambda +10)(\lambda )(\lambda -20) & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +10)(\lambda -20) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-36831.name: Question 2
q-36831.problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$B=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$
q-36831.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,B-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
B-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(B-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Since the determinant of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix is given by the product of the entries on the main diagonal, we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )(1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -4)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$

**Note:** The eigenvalues of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix are always the entries on the main diagonal.

EXPLANATION

First, we find the matrix B−λI: ﻿﻿﻿B−λI=[−1−λ0024−λ0001−λ]

The characteristic equation is det(B−λI)=0.

Since the determinant of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix is given by the product of the entries on the main diagonal, we obtain the following:

$$

Find the characteristic equation of the matrix A=[−32−1523001].

a
(1−λ)(λ2+λ+4)=0
b
(1−λ)(λ2+λ−16)=0
c
(1−λ)(λ2+λ−4)=0
d
(1−λ)(λ2+λ−10)=0
e
(1−λ)(λ2−16)=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the matrix A−λI: ﻿﻿﻿A−λI=[−3−λ2−152−λ3001−λ]

The characteristic equation is det(A−λI)=0.

Expanding the determinant across the 3rd row, we obtain the following:

det(A−λI)=0|−3−λ2−152−λ3001−λ|=0(1−λ)|−3−λ252−λ|=0(1−λ)((−3−λ)(2−λ)−2⋅5)=0(1−λ)(λ2+λ−16)=0

q-80553.name: Question 5
q-80553.problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$B=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].$
q-80553.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,B-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
B-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & -4-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(B-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Since the determinant of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix is given by the product of the entries on the main diagonal, we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & -4-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )(5-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda +4)(\lambda -5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$

**Note:** The eigenvalues of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix are always the entries on the main diagonal.

﻿﻿﻿

$$

$$

$$

q-86752.name: Question 8
q-86752.problem:
$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -7\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $D$ given above. Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\lambda =2$ is an eigenvalue of $D$

II. $\lambda =-1$ is an eigenvalue of $D$

III. The eigenvalue $\lambda =-1$ has algebraic multiplicity $2$
q-86752.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,D-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
D-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & -2 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -\lambda  & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -7-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(D-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Notice that we can expand the $4\times 4$ determinant across the $1$st column, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(D-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & -2 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -\lambda  & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & -\lambda  & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, expanding the $3\times 3$ determinant across the $3$rd row, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1-\lambda )(-7-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -1 \\ -2 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(-7-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(-\lambda )-2) & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda +7)({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2) & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda +7)(\lambda -2)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2}(\lambda +7)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $D$ are $\lambda =-1$ (with algebraic multiplicity $2$), $\lambda =-7$ and $\lambda =2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

q-37353.name: Question 10
q-37353.problem:
Find the characteristic equation of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].$
q-37353.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -1-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 4-\lambda  & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}].
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Since the determinant of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix is given by the product of the entries on the main diagonal, we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -1-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 4-\lambda  & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(-1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )(1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (\lambda -5)(\lambda +1)(\lambda -4)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-140475.name: Question 11
q-140475.problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].$
q-140475.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 2 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}|-(-1)|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}|+(-1)|\begin{aligned}1 & -3-\lambda  \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+15\lambda )+(-5-\lambda )+(5+\lambda ) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+13\lambda -10 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $10:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 5,\pm 10
$$

Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}+2(1)^{2}-13(1)+10 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is a root of the equation. So, we can factor $(\lambda -1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +10$ using synthetic division:

| $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-13$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $3$ | $-10$ |
|  | $1$ | $3$ | $-10$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -1)({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -10) & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +5)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-5,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=2.$

q-140515.problem:
Find the characteristic equation of the matrix 
$C=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].$
q-140515.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,C-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
C-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(C-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(C-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 2 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}|-(-1)|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}|+(-1)|\begin{aligned}1 & -3-\lambda  \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+5\lambda )+(-\lambda -5)-(5+\lambda ) & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+15\lambda )-\lambda -5-5-\lambda  & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+13\lambda -10 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-80825.problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}].$
q-80825.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}+6\lambda +5)-(-1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}+7\lambda +6 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $6:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 3,\pm 6
$$

- Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}-7(1)-6 & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is not a root of the equation.

- Let's pick $x=-1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{3}-7(-1)-6 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-1$ is a root of the equation.

So, we can factor $(\lambda +1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6$ using synthetic division:

| $-1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-7$ | $-6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $6$ |
|  | $1$ | $-1$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +1)({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6) & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.$
